items.summary: The question asks about two different services at once; the rewrite splits it into one satisfaction question for recycling services and one for street cleaning.

flags.why: A respondent happy with one service and unhappy with the other has no true answer. A single rating mixes two objects.
Respondents may think of kerb collection, drop-off sites or bins differently. The brief does not say which is meant.
Respondents who do not use a service or cannot judge it have no clear option, so they may pick the midpoint.

rewrite.intro: These questions are about services provided by your local council.
rewrite.stem: How satisfied or dissatisfied are you with the recycling services provided by your local council?
options: Don't know or no experience of this service
rewrite.programming: Ask as two separate questions on separate screens. Q1a: recycling services. Q1b: same stem and options, with 'street cleaning' in place of 'recycling services'. Same option order and labels for both. [Analyst to decide what recycling services covers.]

items.summary: "Financial situation" is open: it could mean income, savings, debts, the respondent or the household. The rewrite names whose situation and what it covers, using placeholders.

flags.why: Respondents may think of income, savings, debts or spending, and of themselves or their household. Each reads the phrase differently, so answers are not comparable.
The ends differ in kind and strength: "comfortably" has no intensity word, while "very difficult" does. The in-between options were not shown, so balance cannot be fully checked.

rewrite.intro: Think about [what it covers, e.g. income, savings and debts].
rewrite.stem: How would you describe [your own / your household's] financial situation at the moment?

items.summary: Asks respondents to add two activity types over an undefined 'typical week' with undefined terms; the rewrite splits them, defines the terms and uses the last 7 days.

flags.quote: vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity combined
flags.why: Respondents must work out hours for two kinds of activity and add them in their head. Two different things are asked at once.

flags.quote: vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity
flags.why: Respondents will draw the line between vigorous and moderate differently. It is also unclear whether work, housework or walking count.
'Typical' has no clear start or end. Respondents must average over varying weeks, so each person builds the answer differently.
Categories are not shown, so fit cannot be judged. Respondents read the scale as what is normal; the top may be too low or too high.

rewrite.intro: Think about the last 7 days, from [start day] up to today. Vigorous activity means [definition of vigorous activity]. Moderate activity means [definition of moderate activity].
rewrite.stem: Q1a. In the last 7 days, how many hours did you spend doing vigorous physical activity? Q1b. In the last 7 days, how many hours did you spend doing moderate physical activity?
options: [categories between None and More than 10 hours, as in the original scale]
rewrite.programming: Same options for Q1a and Q1b. Definitions in the intro must be on screen with the questions. Categories between the end points are not shown in the test.

items.summary: Loaded premise, negative lead-in, two targets and one-sided agree-disagree wording; rewrite asks one balanced question on the number of immigrants, with direction options.

flags.quote: Given the growing pressure on public services
flags.why: States a contested claim as fact and pushes respondents toward agreeing with reduction before they judge the issue themselves.
Negative, leading question form combined with agree-disagree options; it is unclear whether agreeing means yes or no to the idea.

flags.quote: particularly those who may not contribute to the economy
flags.why: Adds a second target: all immigrants versus only some. A respondent who wants fewer of one group but not the other cannot answer.

flags.quote: should do more to reduce the number of immigrants
flags.why: Only the reduction position is stated. Respondents who want the number kept or increased are not offered their view in the stem.
The statement holds a quantity and a direction, so agree-disagree adds acquiescence risk and makes respondents answer two things at once.
Vague: it could mean tougher laws, tighter borders or something else. 'Immigrants' and 'may not contribute' also have open boundaries.
No don't-know option is shown, so respondents with no view may be pushed to invent one. Confirm one is offered.

rewrite.intro: Immigrants are people who come from other countries to live in [country] for [period].
rewrite.stem: Do you think the number of immigrants coming to this country should be increased, reduced, or kept about the same?
rewrite.programming: Show every option label on screen. [Define immigrant and the period in the intro.]

items.summary: Assumes a paid job, 'terms of employment' is unclear, and the scale is unbalanced; rewrite adds a job filter, a definition and a balanced scale.

flags.why: Adults who are unemployed, retired, studying or not in paid work have no terms of employment to rate and cannot answer truthfully.
Some will think of pay, others of hours, contract type or leave. The phrase does not say what counts, so people rate different things.

flags.quote: Completely satisfied / Very satisfied / Fairly satisfied / Not very satisfied / Not at all satisfied
flags.why: Three positive points against two negative ones, with no middle option and no 'dissatisfied' wording. Neutral or mildly unhappy people have no matching answer.

rewrite.intro: These questions are about your current paid job. By terms of employment we mean [analyst to list what is covered, e.g. pay, working hours, type of contract, leave].
rewrite.stem: Overall, how satisfied or dissatisfied are you with your terms of employment?
rewrite.programming: Add a filter question before Q1, e.g. 'Do you currently have a paid job?' Yes / No. Ask Q1 only if Yes; if No, skip Q1. Show the definition on the same screen as the question.

items.summary: Household, income sources and 'deductions' are undefined, and respondents must add up several people's pay. The rewrite defines household and income, uses last month, and asks about tax only.

flags.quote: your household's total monthly income from all sources
flags.why: It does not say who counts as the household or which money counts as income (pay, benefits, pensions, gifts, savings interest).

flags.quote: total monthly income from all sources
flags.why: Respondent must add several people's money from several sources, and convert weekly or yearly pay to a month. Others' income may be unknown.
'Deductions' is vague and joins two things. Many people know only take-home pay, so they may report that instead.
Income is private; some people may skip or understate it. The shown options include no don't-know or prefer-not-to-say route. Middle options were not shown.

rewrite.intro: Count money from work, benefits, pensions and any other source for [people counted as the household].
rewrite.stem: What was your household's total income last month, before tax was taken off?
options: [options in between, as in the original]

items.summary: The item asks about work and services at once and assumes everyone works; the rewrite splits it into two questions and adds a not-applicable option.

flags.quote: to get to work and to access essential services such as healthcare
flags.why: Two different things are asked at once. A person for whom work is easy to reach but healthcare is hard has no single true answer.
Retired people, unemployed people, people working from home and others do not travel to work. No not-applicable option is offered, so they must guess or skip.
Which services count is left open. Respondents will think of different ones. 'Access' could mean distance, cost, waiting time or transport.
Ease depends on how a person travels (car, bus, walking) and when. Respondents will judge on different bases unless the analyst fixes the travel meaning.

rewrite.intro: The next question is about travel to work.
rewrite.stem: How easy or difficult is it for you to travel from your home to your place of work?
options: [middle options as in the original scale]
I do not travel to a workplace
rewrite.programming: Scale from Very easy to Very difficult as in the original, with the not-applicable option last. Ask a second question after this one: 'How easy or difficult is it for you to travel from your home to the nearest [health service: analyst to define, e.g. doctor or health centre]?' Same scale, no not-applicable option. Add one such question for each further service the analyst needs.

items.summary: Social media is undefined, no week is stated, and weekly hours must be added up in the head; the rewrite defines the term and asks for each of the last 7 days.

flags.why: The term has an open boundary. Respondents may or may not count messaging apps, video sites or forums, so they answer about different things.
It is unclear which week is meant: the last 7 days, a typical week, or the current calendar week. Respondents will choose differently.

flags.quote: how many hours per week do you spend
flags.why: Frequent, scattered use must be added across days and platforms and turned into hours. Respondents will guess or round.
The middle options are not shown, so exhaustiveness cannot be judged. The top category is about 3 hours a day and cuts off heavy users.

rewrite.intro: Think about the last 7 days, up to and including yesterday. Social media means [definition or examples of what counts]. Include time on any device.
rewrite.stem: How much time did you spend on social media on each of these days?
rewrite.open_format: Hours and minutes for each day; 0 is an allowed answer.
rewrite.programming: Web: one entry per day; allowed range 0 to 24 hours per day; weekday labels filled from today's date; the analyst sums the days.

items.summary: The statement mixes moral desert, severe punishment and longer prison terms in one leading, one-sided claim; the rewrite asks only about sentence length with balanced options.

flags.quote: deserve to be punished severely, even if this means longer prison sentences
flags.why: Asks about what people deserve, how harsh punishment should be, and longer prison terms at once. A respondent may want to answer each part differently.

flags.quote: even if this means longer prison sentences
flags.why: The 'even if' clause treats longer sentences as an accepted cost and pushes toward agreement. 'Deserve' adds a moral push.

flags.quote: People who commit serious crimes deserve to be punished severely
flags.why: Only the harsher position is stated. The opposite position (lighter or shorter punishment) is not in the stem.
Respondents will picture different offences. 'Severely' is also vague: it could mean prison length, prison conditions or other penalties.

flags.quote: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
flags.why: Agree-disagree invites acquiescence. Options in the construct's own terms (shorter or longer sentences) would measure the view more directly.

flags.quote: a scale running from Strongly agree to Strongly disagree
flags.why: No don't-know or no-opinion option is shown. Respondents with no firm view on sentencing may have to invent an answer.

rewrite.intro: Think about people found guilty of [serious crimes: analyst to define which offences].
rewrite.stem: In your view, should prison sentences for these people be longer, shorter, or about the same as they are now?
rewrite.programming: Show all option labels on screen. Don't know is a visible option, set apart from the scale.

items.summary: The question asks about day and after dark together, so the rewrite splits it into two questions on the same scale.

flags.quote: during the day and after dark
flags.why: Someone who feels safe by day but unsafe at night has no single true answer. The two times need separate answers.
The edge of a neighbourhood is open. Respondents may picture their street, a few blocks or the wider district, which may change answers.
Some people never go out after dark. They must imagine it or guess. Dark falls at different hours by season. Depends on what the analyst wants measured.

rewrite.stem: Q1a. How safe do you feel in your neighbourhood during the day? Q1b. How safe do you feel in your neighbourhood after dark?
options: [intermediate options as in the original scale]
rewrite.programming: Ask Q1a and Q1b as two separate questions, each with the same scale. Options between Very safe and Very unsafe were not shown in the test and stay as in the original.

items.summary: "Healthcare professional" is open-ended and there is no answer for people who needed no appointment; the rewrite names what counts and adds that option.

flags.why: Respondents may think of a family doctor, a specialist, a nurse, a dentist or a pharmacist. The boundary is open, so answers refer to different things.
Someone who needed no appointment in the past 12 months has no true answer on this scale. They must skip, guess or pick a false point.
Respondents with several appointments or needs over a year must average mixed experiences into one rating. Recent or memorable ones may dominate.

rewrite.intro: This question is about [list of healthcare professionals that count, to be set by the analyst].
rewrite.stem: In the past 12 months, how easy was it to get an appointment when you needed one?
options: I did not need an appointment in the past 12 months
rewrite.programming: Middle scale labels were not shown in the original; the analyst should confirm them. Show all labels on screen. Insert the list of professionals in the lead-in.

items.summary: Opening sentence states a research claim as fact and pushes answers; the rewrite removes it and adds a placeholder defining 'stay at home'.

flags.quote: Research consistently shows that children benefit from having a parent at home in the early years.
flags.why: States a claim as fact and appeals to research. This pushes respondents toward 'important' and gives them a reason before they form their own view.
Could mean being at home all day, not doing paid work, or working from home. Respondents will picture different arrangements.
The lead-in speaks of 'a parent' but the question asks only about mothers. Whether the question should cover mothers only, fathers, or either parent is the analyst's decision.

rewrite.intro: Think about children who are not yet at school. By 'stay at home' we mean [what staying at home covers, e.g. not in paid work].
rewrite.stem: How important do you think it is that mothers stay at home to look after their children before they start school?

items.summary: No fix-level fault found. The idiom 'the way things are going' and the time frame 'at this moment' may be read differently, which is for the analyst to decide.

flags.quote: the way things are going in your life
flags.why: This idiom can mean how life is now or which direction it is heading. Respondents may answer different questions.
Some respondents may judge their mood right now, others their life these days. The time frame has no clear boundaries.
Only the end points are labelled, so the middle points are open to different readings. This is a defensible design choice.

items.summary: Asks about availability and affordability together, and has no route for people with no experience of childcare. The rewrite splits it into two questions and adds a 'Does not apply to me' option.

flags.why: A respondent may be happy with how many places exist but unhappy with the cost. One answer cannot show both.

flags.quote: How satisfied are you with the availability and affordability of childcare services in your area?
flags.why: Assumes everyone has a view of childcare. People with no children or no need for it have no option to say so and may guess.
It is unclear what counts: nurseries, childminders, after-school care, or help from relatives. Respondents may picture different things.
Respondents may take 'area' as street, town or region, so the place they judge differs.

rewrite.intro: Think about childcare services in [local area, define as needed]. Childcare services means [what counts as childcare, to be defined by the analyst].
rewrite.stem: Q1a. How satisfied are you with the availability of childcare services? Q1b. How satisfied are you with the cost of childcare services?
options: [in-between options as in the original scale]
rewrite.programming: Show Q1a and Q1b on separate screens with the same options. The analyst decides whether a filter on childcare experience is also needed.

items.summary: Leading premises, the unexplained term 'carbon footprint', a long stem and a vague 'past year' are the main faults; the rewrite removes the premises, defines the term and fixes the period.

flags.quote: Considering the urgent need to address climate change and the fact that individual actions collectively make a significant difference
flags.why: States contested claims as fact and pushes respondents to report changes. It also assumes they accept those claims.
A technical term. Respondents may not know what it covers, so each may picture different actions.

flags.quote: to what extent have you made changes to your daily habits specifically to reduce your personal carbon footprint over the past year
flags.why: A long stem with a premise clause and several qualifiers. Respondents may lose the core question.
Start and end are not stated. Respondents may count a calendar year, 12 months, or a different span.
Unclear which habits count (energy, travel, food, shopping) and how big a change must be. Respondents will each pick their own.
People who already lived in a low-carbon way before the period cannot truthfully say they made changes, so this answer misdescribes them.

flags.quote: A great deal to Not at all
flags.why: Middle options were not shown, so labelling, midpoint and balance cannot be judged. Confirm that all points are labelled and evenly spaced.

flags.quote: individual actions collectively make a significant difference
flags.why: This framing makes a low answer look unfavourable, so respondents who made few changes may over-report.

rewrite.intro: Think about the last 12 months, up to today. [Short definition of 'carbon footprint' and what it covers, to be chosen by the analyst.]
rewrite.stem: How much have you changed your daily habits to reduce your carbon footprint?
options: [intermediate options as in the original test version]

items.summary: Unclear what counts as volunteering, which organisations count, and which year; the rewrite defines these and asks for a number of days in an open field.

flags.why: Voluntary work and unpaid work are different things. Unpaid work could mean a family business or an internship, so respondents may count different activities.
Unclear what counts: a church, a sports club, a school group or a charity. Respondents will draw the line in different places.
No start or end point is given. Respondents may think of the calendar year or the last 12 months, and recall fades over that span.
'Times' is not defined (day, session or task). Regular volunteers cannot count each occasion over a year and must guess.
The top category is low for regular volunteers, who may read it as the norm. The middle options were not shown, so they could not be checked.

rewrite.intro: Unpaid volunteer work means [definition of what counts, with examples of organisations]. Think about the time from [start date] to today.
rewrite.stem: On how many days did you do unpaid volunteer work for a [community organisation as defined] in that time?
rewrite.open_format: Whole number of days; enter 0 if none.
rewrite.programming: Open numeric field; allowed range 0 to [maximum days in the period].

items.summary: Stem asks how adequate the space is but options say too much or too little; rewrite asks directly how much space there is.

flags.quote: How adequate is the amount of space
flags.why: The stem asks about adequacy, but the options run from too much to too little. Respondents cannot tell whether 'far too much' counts as adequate.
Space could mean floor area, number of rooms, storage or outdoor areas. Respondents may each think of something different.
Members of a household may have different needs, and respondents must decide whose needs to weigh. This depends on what the analyst wants measured.

rewrite.intro: Think about the space inside the home where you live now. [Analyst to state what counts as space, such as rooms or storage.]
rewrite.stem: How much space does your home have for your household?
options: About the right amount of space

items.summary: Asks about two topics at once, assumes a partner and children, and gives no time frame. The rewrite asks about money alone, adds a period, filters and an open count.

flags.quote: argue about money and about how to raise your children
flags.why: Two topics in one question. A respondent who argues often about money but rarely about children has no single true answer.
Assumes the respondent has a partner. Single respondents have no true answer, and 'partner' may be read as a business partner or a spouse only.
Assumes the respondent has children to raise. Respondents without children, or with grown children, cannot answer truthfully.

flags.quote: How often do you and your partner argue
flags.why: No time frame. Respondents choose their own period, such as this week or the whole relationship, so answers are not comparable.

flags.quote: a scale running from Very often to Never
flags.why: 'Very often' and similar words mean different frequencies to different people. The middle options are not shown, so balance and labels could not be checked.
Could mean any disagreement or only raised voices. Respondents may set the threshold differently. The analyst may want to say what counts.

rewrite.intro: Think about the last [reference period, e.g. 4 weeks]. By partner we mean [definition of partner, e.g. husband, wife, or the person you live with as a couple].
rewrite.stem: How many times did you and your partner argue about money?
rewrite.open_format: Whole number of times in the reference period; 0 is a valid answer.
rewrite.programming: Filter first: 'Do you currently have a partner?' (Yes/No); ask this question only if Yes. Then ask the same question about 'how to raise your children' only of respondents who have a child [definition, e.g. child under 18 living at home]. Allowed range 0 to [maximum].

items.summary: The lead-in presents scandals as fact and pushes answers down, and 'politicians' is unbounded; the rewrite drops the lead-in and names the group.

flags.quote: Given the recent scandals in government
flags.why: States scandals as fact and primes a negative view. Respondents may also read 'recent' and 'scandals' differently, so answers lean toward low trust.

flags.quote: trust do you have in politicians
flags.why: 'Politicians' could mean national, local, own party, or all. Respondents will each picture a different group, so answers are not comparable.
'Public interest' is abstract. Respondents may take it to mean the country, their area, or people like them.

rewrite.intro: This question is about [which politicians, for example members of the national parliament].
rewrite.stem: How much do you trust [these politicians] to act in the public interest?

items.summary: Asks for one total across many activities, with a long list of inclusions and exclusions and a vague 'typical' day; the rewrite asks per activity for one named weekday.

flags.quote: socialising, watching television, reading, or using the internet for personal enjoyment
flags.why: Respondent must recall several different activities and add their hours in their head to give one total.

flags.quote: not including time spent on domestic tasks, caring responsibilities, or personal grooming, but including any time spent on hobbies
flags.why: One long sentence with stacked exclusions and inclusions is hard to hold in mind while answering.

flags.quote: not including time spent on domestic tasks
flags.why: The exclusion is worded as a negation inside a long sentence, so respondents may miss it or apply it unevenly.
The boundary is open: hobbies such as cooking or gardening may count as domestic tasks, and the internet may overlap with TV or socialising.
'Typical' is undefined; respondents with varying days or shifts must average in their head, and the day is not named.
The top category may be too low for some people, such as retired or unemployed respondents; the middle options were not shown, so exhaustiveness could not be checked.

rewrite.intro: Think about [the most recent weekday, Monday to Friday]. Count each hour only once.
rewrite.stem: How many hours did you spend on each of these activities on that day?
rows: Using the internet for personal enjoyment
rewrite.open_format: Number of hours for each row, in hours (allow 0), with one entry field per row
rewrite.programming: Numeric entry 0–24 per row; check that the rows do not sum to more than 24 hours; the analyst sums rows if a total is needed. [Define the reference weekday.]

items.summary: No fix-level fault found by this review; the time frame and the labels on only the two end points are design choices for the analyst to decide.

flags.quote: how happy would you say you are
flags.why: No time frame is given. Some respondents may rate their mood today, others their life these days, so answers may not be comparable. Depends on the intended construct.
Only the end points have labels, so respondents may read the middle points differently. A defensible choice; the brief gives no analysis need.

items.summary: The word 'politics' is open and could be read as party politics, government or local issues. Only consider-level flags, so no rewrite.

flags.why: Respondents may think of parties, government, local issues or world events. A short definition would give everyone the same object in mind; the analyst decides what it covers.
'Quite' can mean 'fairly' or 'very', and 'hardly' is less common. Respondents may place the middle labels differently.

items.summary: No fault that needs a fix was found by this review; two design choices are noted: the open time frame and the label "Fair". No rewrite.

flags.why: No time frame or comparison standard is given. Respondents may think of today, the past year, or people their own age, and may mean body or mind.
"Fair" may read as mildly positive or as the middle. The scale then has an uneven midpoint, which can shift answers toward the good end.

items.summary: No fix-level fault found by this review; the only note is that 'nowadays' leaves the time frame open, which is a design choice. No rewrite.

flags.why: 'Nowadays' has no clear start point. Some respondents may think of this week, others of this year, so they may judge different periods.

items.summary: No fix-level fault found; two design choices to consider: the broad object 'climate change' and no no-opinion option.

flags.why: Respondents may think of different things: the global process, local weather, or effects on themselves. Worry about each could differ. A short definition or a narrower object may help.

flags.quote: Not at all worried to Extremely worried
flags.why: No visible route for people with no view or little knowledge. They may choose a scale point they have not really formed. Whether to add one depends on your aims.

items.summary: No time frame and unclear what counts as fruit; the rewrite adds a [reference period] and a definition of fruit, and moves the juice exclusion into a lead-in.

flags.quote: How often do you eat fruit
flags.why: No time frame is given. Respondents choose their own period (typical day, recent week, whole year), so answers are not comparable.
The boundary is open. Fresh, dried, canned, fruit in cooked dishes or yoghurt, and smoothies may or may not be counted.
The exclusion trails after the main question and is awkward. Respondents may miss it, or be unsure whether other fruit drinks are also excluded.

flags.quote: a scale running from Three times or more a day to Never
flags.why: The middle options were not shown, so they were not assessed. Check that the units stay consistent and the categories do not overlap.

rewrite.intro: Think about [reference period]. Fruit means [what counts as fruit, e.g. fresh, dried, canned]. Leave out fruit juice.
rewrite.stem: How often did you eat fruit in [reference period]?
options: Three times or more a day
[options in between, as in the original]

items.summary: No fix-level fault found by this review; main concern is that 'life in general nowadays' covers no defined area or time span, so no rewrite.

flags.quote: over your life in general nowadays
flags.why: Respondents may think of different parts of life (work, money, health) and different time spans, since 'nowadays' has no start point.
Only the end points are labelled, so respondents may read the nine middle points differently. A defensible design choice if comparability with other data matters.
